questions.statement: You write to your head teacher. Which greeting starts the email formally?
questions.context: Lucia is learning formal and informal email styles in class.

options.text: Dear Mrs Lopez,
options.feedback: Correct! Dear Mrs Lopez is formal because Dear plus title plus surname shows respect suited to a teacher or office.

options.text: Hi Lucia,
options.feedback: The greeting Hi Lucia is wrong as formal because Hi plus first name is friendly and informal, not respectful for officials.

options.text: Yo guys, listen up,
options.feedback: The greeting Yo guys, listen up is wrong because slang plus order is very informal and rude for any formal email.

options.text: Starting with no greeting at all.
options.feedback: Starting with no greeting is wrong because opening without salutation looks careless and never meets formal email rules.

questions.explanation: Formal greetings use Dear plus title and surname, such as Dear Mrs Lopez. Informal greetings use Hi or Hello plus first name for friends.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: You finish a formal complaint to a company. Which closing is correct?
questions.context: Marco is studying polite closings for different email types.

options.text: Yours faithfully, Pablo Ruiz.
options.feedback: Correct! Yours faithfully is formal closing because it matches official letters and pairs with a full name signature.

options.text: Lots of love, Pablo.
options.feedback: The closing Lots of love is wrong as formal because it expresses affection suited to close friends, not to officials.

options.text: Cheers mate, Pablo.
options.feedback: The closing Cheers mate is wrong as formal because Cheers plus mate is casual slang for friends, not for formal mail.

options.text: No closing and no signature.
options.feedback: Closing with no signature is wrong because ending without a name looks incomplete and unprofessional in any formal message.

questions.explanation: Formal closings include Yours faithfully or Yours sincerely plus full name. Informal closings use Best wishes, Cheers or Lots of love.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: You email the office for a certificate. Which subject line is formal and clear?
questions.context: Sara is learning to choose the right subject line.

options.text: Request for school certificate, 12 May.
options.feedback: Correct! Request for school certificate, 12 May is clear because it names the exact request plus a date for the office to process.

options.text: Hey you, open this fast.
options.feedback: The subject Hey you is wrong because vague slang gives no clue about content and looks unprofessional in an inbox.

options.text: Funny cats video inside.
options.feedback: The subject Funny cats video is wrong because cats are unrelated to a certificate and mislead the office staff completely.

options.text: Leaving the subject line blank.
options.feedback: Leaving the subject blank is wrong because empty subjects force readers to guess and often send mail to spam folders.

questions.explanation: Subject lines summarise the email purpose in a few clear words. Formal subjects name request plus date, while vague hellos confuse readers.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: You ask a language school for details. Which request sentence is formal?
questions.context: Pablo is practising formal requests in emails.

options.text: I am writing to request information about courses.
options.feedback: Correct! I am writing to request information about courses is formal because the full purpose phrase plus polite noun shows respectful structure.

options.text: Send me course info right now.
options.feedback: The demand Send me course info now is wrong because the imperative plus now sounds like an order and lacks formal softening.

options.text: Gimme stuff about those courses.
options.feedback: The slang Gimme stuff about courses is wrong because Gimme is very informal slang that destroys any formal tone instantly.

options.text: Do you like courses or not?
options.feedback: The question Do you like courses or not is wrong because asking personal taste never requests course information formally.

questions.explanation: Formal requests use I am writing to plus infinitive and polite modals like Could you. Short demands like Send me lack courtesy and structure.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which apology sentence suits a formal email to a teacher?
questions.context: Elena is comparing contractions in formal and informal mail.

options.text: I am sorry for the delay, I will reply soon.
options.feedback: Correct! I am sorry for the delay, I will reply soon is formal because full forms plus apology keep a respectful professional tone.

options.text: Gonna reply soon, wanna wait a bit?
options.feedback: The line Gonna reply soon, wanna wait is wrong as formal because gonna and wanna are spoken slang unsuitable for official mail.

options.text: Whatever, chill, we talk later.
options.feedback: The line Whatever, chill, talk later is wrong because dismissal plus slang shows no respect and breaks any formal register.

options.text: Send pics, LOL, bye for now.
options.feedback: The line Send pics, LOL, bye is wrong because text slang plus LOL belongs to chats, not to formal apology emails.

questions.explanation: Formal emails avoid contractions and slang, using I am and I would like. Informal emails accept gonna, wanna and short forms between friends.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: You email your friend Marta about the weekend. Which opening is informal and warm?
questions.context: Diego is writing an informal email to a close friend.

options.text: Hi Marta! Thanks for your message!
options.feedback: Correct! Hi Marta! Thanks for your message! is informal because Hi plus first name plus exclamation shows warm friendly tone.

options.text: Dear Sir or Madam,
options.feedback: The formal Dear Sir or Madam is wrong as friendly because Dear Sir is distant and cold when writing to a close friend.

options.text: I remain your obedient servant,
options.feedback: The sentence I remain your obedient servant is wrong because ancient formal phrases sound comic and stiff between young friends.

options.text: Please acknowledge receipt of this message.
options.feedback: The demand Acknowledge receipt of this message is wrong because office language about receipt is cold and unsuitable for friends.

questions.explanation: Informal emails to friends use Hi, contractions, exclamation and warm closings. Overly stiff Dear Sir language sounds distant between friends.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Your new phone broke in two days. Which opening starts a formal complaint well?
questions.context: Carmen is learning how to start a formal complaint email.

options.text: I am writing to complain about the broken phone.
options.feedback: Correct! I am writing to complain about the broken phone is effective because it names purpose plus faulty item calmly and clearly.

options.text: You thieves stole my money, fix it.
options.feedback: The insult You thieves stole my money is wrong because accusations plus anger sound aggressive and weaken a formal complaint.

options.text: My phone loves flying off tables, haha.
options.feedback: The joke My phone loves flying off tables is wrong because humour hides the problem and gives no clear complaint facts.

options.text: Your shop is the best in the city.
options.feedback: The praise Your shop is the best ever is wrong because compliments cannot complain about a broken phone and confuse the reader.

questions.explanation: Complaints state the problem politely with I am writing to complain about plus facts. Angry insults weaken the case and may be ignored.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence ends a formal email politely before the signature?
questions.context: Andres is practising polite endings before a signature.

options.text: Thank you for your time and kind attention.
options.feedback: Correct! Thank you for your time and kind attention is polite because thanks plus attention shows gratitude before the formal signature.

options.text: Reply now or I will report you.
options.feedback: The demand Reply now or I will report you is wrong because threats plus urgency destroy politeness before the signature.

options.text: Later dude, catch you soon.
options.feedback: The slang Later dude, catch you soon is wrong because dude plus catch you is casual chat, not a polite formal ending.

options.text: Ending with no thanks at all.
options.feedback: Ending with no thanks at all is wrong because closing without gratitude sounds cold and incomplete in formal correspondence.

questions.explanation: Polite formal endings thank the reader and promise contact, such as Thank you for your time. Rude endings demand fast action without thanks.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Formal complaint draft includes four lines. Which line breaks formal register?
questions.context: Lucia is identifying register mistakes in student drafts.

options.text: I wanna ask for a refund ASAP.
options.feedback: Correct! I wanna ask for a refund ASAP is the mistake because wanna plus ASAP slang clashes with the formal complaint purpose.

options.text: I am writing to request a refund.
options.feedback: The phrase I am writing to request a refund is not a mistake because full forms plus request keep a consistent formal register.

options.text: Please find my receipt attached.
options.feedback: The phrase Please find my receipt attached is not a mistake because polite please plus attached follows standard formal conventions.

options.text: Yours sincerely, Lucia Gomez.
options.feedback: The phrase Yours sincerely with full name is not a mistake because the classic closing correctly finishes a formal complaint.

questions.explanation: Register mistakes mix slang into formal mail. Wanna and gonna clash with Dear Sir openings, while full forms keep the tone consistent.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: You invite friends by email to your party. Which line is informal and natural?
questions.context: Marco is reviewing opening lines for informal invitations.

options.text: Come to my party on Saturday, it will be great!
options.feedback: Correct! Come to my party on Saturday, it will be great is informal because the direct invite plus will be great sounds warm and friendly.

options.text: You are cordially invited to attend the gala.
options.feedback: The formal You are cordially invited to attend is wrong as informal because cordially plus attend is stiff and ceremonial for friends.

options.text: Staff must confirm attendance in writing.
options.feedback: The office line Staff must confirm attendance in writing is wrong because must plus in writing is bureaucratic, not a friendly invite.

options.text: Something maybe happens sometime soon.
options.feedback: The vague Something maybe happens sometime is wrong because vagueness gives no clear invitation details for the party.

questions.explanation: Informal invitations are direct and warm with You are invited plus contractions. Formal notices use passive structures and full titles instead.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: You apply for a summer job. Which opening sentence is formal and strong?
questions.context: Sara is choosing formal language for job applications.

options.text: I would like to apply for the assistant post.
options.feedback: Correct! I would like to apply for the assistant post is formal because would like plus post names the goal with respectful grammar.

options.text: I wanna get that job, so call me.
options.feedback: The slang I wanna get that job, call me is wrong because wanna plus call me sounds like a text to friends, not an application.

options.text: I am the coolest person alive today.
options.feedback: The joke I am the coolest person alive is wrong because boasting plus coolest gives no skills and breaks formal self presentation.

options.text: Do you pay well for this job?
options.feedback: The question Do you pay well for this job is wrong as opening because asking salary first ignores skills and sounds impolite.

questions.explanation: Job applications need formal self presentation with I would like to apply and I attach my CV. Casual chat about bands harms the candidate image.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which line is too informal for a message to the school office? Choose the informal one.
questions.context: Pablo is correcting abbreviations in formal emails.

options.text: BTW, send me the file ASAP, thx.
options.feedback: Correct! BTW, send me the file ASAP, thx is informal because BTW plus ASAP plus thx are text abbreviations unsuitable for formal mail.

options.text: Please send the file at your convenience.
options.feedback: The sentence Please send the file at your convenience is formal, not informal, because please plus convenience keeps full respectful wording.

options.text: I attach the report for your review.
options.feedback: The sentence I attach the report for your review is formal because attach plus review uses complete professional vocabulary.

options.text: Thank you for your prompt reply.
options.feedback: The sentence Thank you for your prompt reply is formal because thank you plus prompt reply shows full polite business language.

questions.explanation: Formal emails write words in full and avoid text forms like BTW, LOL or u. Informal chats accept them, but offices expect complete spelling.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sequence organises a formal request email correctly?
questions.context: Elena is judging paragraph order in a formal email.

options.text: Greeting, purpose, details, polite close.
options.feedback: Correct! Greeting, purpose, details, polite close is logical because each step prepares the next and respects formal reader expectations.

options.text: Threats, demands, insults, no signature.
options.feedback: The order starting with threats is wrong because threats first alarm readers before any purpose or details are explained.

options.text: Joke, meme, gossip, sudden request.
options.feedback: The order starting with jokes is wrong because humour first hides purpose and undermines the serious formal request.

options.text: No greeting, random details, abrupt end.
options.feedback: The order with no greeting at all is wrong because missing salutation breaks formal structure from the very first line.

questions.explanation: Formal emails order ideas as greeting, purpose, details, polite close. Asking for money before stating purpose confuses and offends readers.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Email ends: I look forward to hearing from you. What is the function of this line?
questions.context: Diego is analysing the function of I look forward phrases.

options.text: It politely invites a reply and closes formally.
options.feedback: Correct! It politely invites a reply and closes formally is right because look forward to hearing signals respectful expectation of an answer.

options.text: It insults the reader for slow answers.
options.feedback: The claim it insults the reader is wrong because look forward language is courteous and never expresses insult or criticism.

options.text: It tells a funny joke before goodbye.
options.feedback: The claim it tells a joke is wrong because no humour appears and the routine is serious business closing language.

options.text: It orders fast delivery of products.
options.feedback: The claim it orders fast delivery is wrong because no demand or deadline is set and the tone stays inviting, not commanding.

questions.explanation: I look forward to hearing from you politely ends formal mail and invites reply. It uses gerund hearing, a classic formal closing routine.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: You must miss class for a family event. Which permission request is formal?
questions.context: Carmen is writing a formal email asking for permission.

options.text: Could you please allow me to miss class on Friday?
options.feedback: Correct! Could you please allow me to miss Friday is polite because Could you plus please turns permission into a respectful formal request.

options.text: I want Friday off, so give it to me.
options.feedback: The demand I want Friday off, give it is wrong because want plus give it orders the teacher instead of requesting permission.

options.text: Maybe I come on Friday or maybe not.
options.feedback: The vague Maybe I come or maybe not is wrong because vagueness gives no clear request and confuses the permission decision.

options.text: I never miss parties, you know that.
options.feedback: The boast I never miss parties, you know is wrong because boasting about parties is irrelevant and never asks permission formally.

questions.explanation: Permission requests use Could you please allow and Would it be possible. Direct I want statements sound demanding in school correspondence.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Your application arrived late. Which apology fits a formal email best?
questions.context: Andres is comparing two apologies for a late application.

options.text: I apologise for the delay due to illness.
options.feedback: Correct! I apologise for the delay due to illness is strong because apologise plus brief reason plus attached form shows full responsibility.

options.text: Traffic was bad, whatever, here it is.
options.feedback: The excuse Traffic was bad, whatever is wrong because whatever dismisses fault and lacks the formal apology structure needed.

options.text: Sorry I forgot, my dog ate the form.
options.feedback: The joke Sorry I forgot, my dog ate it is wrong because humour plus dog excuse is childish and unsuitable for formal applications.

options.text: Sending late papers with no apology.
options.feedback: The silence with no apology is wrong because sending late papers without any apology looks careless and disrespectful.

questions.explanation: Strong formal apologies admit delay, give a brief reason and show action. Blaming traffic without responsibility sounds weak and informal.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: You email an unknown grants officer. Which style keeps the right tone?
questions.context: Lucia is checking tone in emails to unknown officials.

options.text: Dear Sir or Madam, with neutral tone.
options.feedback: Correct! Dear Sir or Madam with neutral tone is right because the title plus polite distance respects an unknown official correctly.

options.text: Hey man, what is up with you?
options.feedback: The greeting Hey man with slang is wrong because Hey man assumes close friendship and insults an unknown official.

options.text: Kisses, see you soon, my friend.
options.feedback: The closing Kisses, see you soon is wrong because affectionate kisses assume intimacy that is absent with unknown officials.

options.text: Answer fast, I have no time.
options.feedback: The demand Answer fast, I have no time is wrong because rushing plus no time pressures officials rudely instead of respecting them.

questions.explanation: Unknown officials need Dear Sir or Madam plus neutral polite language. First names and kisses assume familiarity that does not exist yet.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: You attach a CV to a job email. Which attachment line is formal?
questions.context: Marco is judging attachments language in formal mail.

options.text: Please find my CV attached for review.
options.feedback: Correct! Please find my CV attached for review is formal because please plus attached plus review follows standard business wording.

options.text: See pics attached, LOL, check them.
options.feedback: The slang See pics attached, LOL is wrong because pics plus LOL are chat abbreviations that break formal attachment language.

options.text: Stuff is somewhere inside this mail.
options.feedback: The vague Stuff is somewhere in the mail is wrong because somewhere gives no clear file reference and sounds careless.

options.text: Open it fast and reply right now.
options.feedback: The order Open it fast and reply now is wrong because fast plus now commands the reader instead of politely signalling an attachment.

questions.explanation: Attachment phrases use Please find attached plus file name. Informal see pics attached lacks the polite structure offices expect.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which description matches a complete and correct formal email?
questions.context: Sara is revising a full formal email for final sending.

options.text: Clear subject, Dear title, purpose, close.
options.feedback: Correct! Clear subject, Dear, purpose, details, close is complete because every formal element appears in logical order for the reader.

options.text: No subject, Hi, random chat, no name.
options.feedback: The version with no subject and Hi is wrong because missing subject plus Hi breaks formal completeness from the very start.

options.text: Slang, emojis and jokes throughout.
options.feedback: The version full of slang and emojis is wrong because slang plus emojis destroy professional tone even if structure looks similar.

options.text: Threats, demands and no signature.
options.feedback: The version with threats and no signature is wrong because threats plus missing name make the mail aggressive and incomplete.

questions.explanation: Full formal emails need clear subject, Dear title, stated purpose, details, polite close and full name. Missing subjects or slang break the whole message.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Formal complaint draft mixes Hey, wanna, ASAP and LOL. Which repair fixes the whole register?
questions.context: Pablo is facing the hardest choice on mixed register repair.

options.text: Dear manager, request, please, Yours sincerely.
options.feedback: Correct! Dear manager, request, please, Yours sincerely fixes all because each informal bit is replaced while keeping the refund content intact.

options.text: Hey manager, refund, LOL, cheers dude.
options.feedback: The fix keeping Hey and LOL is wrong because retaining Hey plus LOL leaves informal greetings and laughter in a formal complaint.

options.text: I wanna refund ASAP, send it now.
options.feedback: The fix keeping wanna and ASAP is wrong because wanna plus ASAP preserve slang abbreviations that still break formal register.

options.text: Give refund or else, no closing line.
options.feedback: The fix with threats and no close is wrong because adding aggression plus dropping the close worsens rather than repairing register.

questions.explanation: Repairing mixed register means replacing every informal bit while keeping content. Only full Dear, purpose, please and Yours sincerely fix all errors together.
questions.subject: ingles
